sections.title: Underwriting Performance by Segment
sections.subtitle: Insurance, Reinsurance and Mortgage are Arch's three underwriting segments

charts.title: Net Premiums Written vs Net Earned Premium

combinedRatio.title: Combined ratio by segment
combinedRatio.content:
The combined ratio is losses and expenses as a percentage of earned premium; below 100% means the segment is underwriting at a profit before investment income.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: all three segments widened in 2026 -- Insurance to the mid-90s, Reinsurance into the high-70s as property-cat pricing softened, and Mortgage into the low-to-mid 20s as it normalises off cycle-high margins -- while every segment stayed profitable.

What to watch:

  • Mortgage's ratio rising fastest off a very low base as the housing cycle normalises
  • Reinsurance widening further as the January 2027 property-cat renewal is expected to cut rates another 10-20%

lossRatio.title: Loss ratio
lossRatio.content:
The loss ratio is incurred losses and loss-adjustment expenses as a percentage of earned premium -- the pure underwriting-cost half of the combined ratio (the rest is expenses).

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: the consolidated loss ratio has run in the low-to-mid 50s through 2026; a jump here, such as Q3 2026's elevated catastrophe losses, flows straight into the combined ratio chart above.

What to watch:

  • Spikes from catastrophe quarters versus the underlying attritional trend
  • Favourable prior-year reserve releases masking current-year deterioration

underwritingIncome.title: Underwriting income by segment
underwritingIncome.content:
Underwriting income is earned premium less losses and underwriting expenses -- profit from risk-taking alone, before investment income.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: Mortgage earns the highest margin per dollar of premium but is shrinking as new mortgage originations stay muted; Reinsurance's deliberate pullback from soft property-cat pricing shows up here as falling income even where the combined ratio still looks healthy.

What to watch:

  • Which segment management is shrinking or growing as the cycle turns
  • Underwriting income versus net investment income -- Arch's other profit engine, not shown here

premiumsWritten.title: Gross premiums written by segment
premiumsWritten.content:
Gross premiums written is the total premium booked on policies issued in the period, before ceding to reinsurers -- the top-line volume measure for an insurer.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: Insurance and Reinsurance are roughly equal in size; Reinsurance's volume is falling as the company deliberately non-renews short-tail property-cat business into the softening cycle, while Insurance grows more steadily and Mortgage stays small.

What to watch:

  • Reinsurance volume decline alongside the combined-ratio chart -- is the shrink paired with margin discipline or just lost business
  • Mortgage's small, declining share reflecting muted new mortgage originations

netPremiums.title: Net premiums written vs net earned premium
netPremiums.content:
Net premiums written is gross premium less what is ceded to reinsurers -- the premium Arch actually retains risk on. Net earned premium recognises that retained premium over the policy term, and is the denominator for the loss and combined ratios above.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: the gap between written and earned in any one period is unearned premium moving on or off the balance sheet, which leads earned premium by a few quarters.

What to watch:

  • Written premium turning down before earned premium does
  • How much of any gap is reinsurance cession strategy versus genuine volume change

bookValue.title: Book value per share
bookValue.content:
Book value per share is shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding -- for an insurer, the closest thing to a per-share NAV, and the metric management itself targets for compounding.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: BVPS compounded from $32.62 (FY2022) to $65.11 (FY2025) through retained underwriting and investment profit, but it also swings with unrealised AOCI marks on the bond portfolio -- Q3 2026 BVPS dipped slightly quarter-over-quarter despite strong operating earnings as rising yields hit the available-for-sale book.

What to watch:

  • BVPS growth net of buybacks (a shrinking share count mechanically lifts it)
  • AOCI swings from interest-rate moves versus genuine retained-earnings growth

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Arch Capital Group Ltd.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
